items.title: Luther's Bible and standard German
items.claim: Martin Luther's complete German Bible was published in which year, and which dialect did it draw on as a base?

options.text: 1534, drawing on the East Central German of the Saxon chancellery

items.reveal_title: 1534, based on chancellery East Central German
items.reveal:
Luther's New Testament appeared in 1522; the complete Bible in 1534. The work spread widely with printing and influenced the form of Standard German over the following centuries.

Mid-19th-century unification of orthography accelerated the standard's reach.
items.why: A widely read religious translation can shape a literary language for centuries.

items.title: Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt
items.claim: Bertolt Brecht's theatre theory is widely translated as 'alienation effect'. What does Verfremdungseffekt specifically aim to do?

options.text: Make audiences identify completely with characters
Disrupt emotional immersion so the audience thinks critically about the social conditions depicted
Make plays as short as possible

items.reveal:
Brecht developed the concept from the late 1920s. Verfremdung is closer to 'making strange' than to ordinary alienation.

The Berliner Ensemble, founded with Helene Weigel in 1949, became its main institutional home.
items.why: Translation choices can shift the apparent meaning of a theoretical term.

items.title: 1996 spelling reform
items.claim: A German spelling reform was agreed in 1996 and implemented in stages. Which change is genuinely part of it?

options.text: Abolition of capital letters on nouns
Replacing ß with ss after short vowels in many words (e.g. dass instead of daß)

items.reveal:
The reform rationalised ss usage according to vowel length, modified some compound spellings and changed comma rules.

Major newspapers reversed and re-adopted parts of the reform in the early 2000s, settling on a revised version by 2006.
items.why: Orthographic reforms often face strong public reaction and partial reversal.
